title: Sampati sees Lanka
hook: a vulture's sight reaches Lanka, and his wings grow back

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati raced his brother toward the sun, then burned his wings to shade him. Ahankara races, love shields.

Where is she? That's the only question that matters now, and Sampati can answer it. Vultures, he tells the monkeys, see very far. We're born with it. Our food is far below us, so our eyes reach far. From this hill I can see a hundred yojanas, across the whole sea. The monkeys turn and look where he's looking. All they can see is water.
screen: `WHERE IS SHE?` → `A VULTURE'S SIGHT.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS.`

segments.voice: Sampati looks south and tells them what he sees. An island, a hundred yojanas away. On it, Lanka, a golden city built by Vishvakarma, the architect of the gods. And in it, kept in Ravana's inner grounds and guarded by rakshasa women, is Sita, dressed in yellow silk, grieving. The answer doesn't come from the armies or the kings. It comes from an old, wingless bird who an hour ago wanted to eat them. Then the old promise comes true. Because Sampati has helped Rama's messengers, his wings begin to grow, right there in front of them. He feels young and strong again, and he tells them: make the effort. Cross the sea. Then he spreads his new wings and flies off to see whether he can still fly. Hindus have a word for what Sampati just did: seva, service. Not a job, not a favor traded, but help given to God's work as a kind of worship. It's why families cook in temple kitchens, sweep the hall before a festival, and serve food at a wedding without being asked. In bhakti, the devotional heart of Hinduism, seva is worship you do with your hands. Many teachers read Sampati's wings this way: he gave the one thing he had left, his eyes, to Rama's cause, and the giving made him whole. Now the monkeys know where Sita is. Between them and her lies a hundred yojanas of open sea, and one question left: who can cross it?
screen: `SITA IN LANKA, ACROSS THE SEA.` · `SAMPATI'S WINGS GROW BACK.` · `SEVA: SERVICE AS WORSHIP.` · `THE GIVING MADE HIM WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze go as far as it can, out a window or to the farthest wall, the way Sampati looked across the sea. Breathe in and let your sight be wide. Then bring it close: what's one small seva within reach today? Washing up after someone else's meal, helping set up at a temple or a community event, carrying something for someone. If you pray, offer it to God as you do it; if not, just do it fully, as a gift.
Sampati. With a vulture's sight he sees Sita in Lanka, a hundred yojanas over the sea, and his wings grow back.
Your line: seva, service offered as worship. Sampati gave what he had, and his wings came back. Tomorrow, who can make the jump? That's day six hundred one.

screen: `DAY 601 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW FAR CAN YOU JUMP?`

howItsDone: The Kishkindha Kanda closes on the shore with the question of who can cross the sea; in recitations, Sampati's vision is the turning point that sends listeners into the Sundara Kanda, which some families recite on its own.
